This work introduces a comprehensive dataset and benchmark designed to evaluate the humor generation capabilities of LLMs.  I am recommending the acceptance of this submission for the following reasons:

* `Large-Scale Dataset`: providing a large dataset featuring 365 cartoons from The New Yorker magazine, accompanied by 2.2 million captions and 250 million human ratings.

* `Comprehensive Analysis of Current LLMs`: Analyzing the performance of state-of-the-art models such as GPT-4 and Claude, highlighting their limitations in generating humorous content when compared to human contestants.

* `Benchmarking RLHF Methods`: Evaluating various RLHF strategies, PPO, DPO, and BoN. These methods aim to refine humor generation in LLMs, providing insights into their effectiveness and potential for future enhancements.

I think the paper makes a nice contribution that the community will find valuable. However, I encourage the authors to think carefully about how to reflect on the comments or resolve the questions from reviewers in the camera-ready version.

Our discussion demonstrates the population level funniness rated by the New Yorker crowd is challenging to achieve and of practical importance. We are aware of [1], which studies funniness on a population level in the psychology literature. Psychological and sociological studies are usually motivated by the practical interests and importance of the topic, so we were simply justifying the motivation of this problem through these lenses too. The mean of the population level ratings are of significant interest to the New Yorker. In addition, it provides significant challenges for current LLMs.

We also want to note that the average rating by the population is different from an mean human participant. In fact, as we showed in our paper, expert judgements are much more aligned with the average rating by the population than any random individual (what we often refer to as "mean human rater"). This is not surprising either, as it is the experts' job to figure out what type of content their audience would prefer the most.

[1] Dunbar, R. I., Launay, J., & Curry, O. (2016). The complexity of jokes is limited by cognitive constraints on mentalizing. Human Nature, 27, 130-140.

Thank you for your further clarification and support of our work. We think the questions are very insightful and we would like to incorporate some of the following discussions in our camera ready.

We agree with the reviewer that aligning a model to any particular dataset is biasing the model. Current LLMs trained on web-scale data and aligned to be a helpful assistant are indeed bland and generic, as attested by our own humor expert as well as the FAccT paper suggested by the reviewer. In fact, our expert favors top human captions in the contest 98% of the time over LLM generated captions. The motivation of establishing a dataset and benchmark based on the new yorker cartoon caption contest is because the new yorker readers are generally sophisticated in humor. The winning captions every week are definitely not bland from experts’ perspectives. Here is an additional qualitative analysis we did when comparing human and LLM generated captions.
- **Missing visual details resulting in LLMs generating out-of-context captions.** As an example, for the cartoon in Figure 2, GPT4o-vision generated “So the alien abduction statistics were right. Malls are the prime hunting grounds!”. This caption does not match the cartoon though, since the aliens look missing and worried. Their bodies look skinny and weak. In other words, they don’t seem to be here to hunt humans.
- **Many generated captions are forms of word/phrase modification and creation.** An example of this caption is “Do they have a Black Hole Friday sale?” from GPT4o-vision. Another example from Claude 3 opus is “I don't see 'Invasion Supplies' listed anywhere...” Both of these captions are inventing new words and phrases to make the caption funny. While these can be somewhat funny, they are usually not rated highly by the new yorker audiences.
- **Winning captions tend to appeal to readers with multiple interpretations through different lenses. LLMs currently lack the ability to produce such captions.** The New Yorker’s editorial pick of the final caption was “Oh sure, now you look at a map.” While this caption makes fun of the aliens blaming each other, it also references the experience of a driver missing the direction but claiming they knew the way. On the contrary, GPT4o-vision generated the caption “We travel light-years, and we still need directions!”, which despite making fun of the characters in the cartoon with the same concept, lacks the relatability from an additional perspective.

Therefore, generating a winning caption needs a lot of improvement in state-of-art LLMs’ capabilities, including understanding of tropes and cultural references, long-horizon reasoning, planning and visual understanding. The recent book https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250333407/yourcaptionhasbeenselected demonstrates the multitude of complexity in writing a winning caption. In our opinion, this is what makes our benchmark challenging and our dataset valuable. Successfully aligning LLMs to generate winning captions would mean large leaps in the capabilities mentioned above, and more importantly, the successful integration of these capabilities.
 
While aligning LLMs to generate winning captions poses significant scientific value and challenges, another practical motivation of collecting our dataset was because the New Yorker magazine wanted to figure out the funniest and most attractable content determined their readers. The New Yorker editors would then choose the winners based on our crowdsourcing effort to be featured in their magazine. We acknowledge that we are studying the very specific genre of the New Yorker humor, which has been lasting over a century. Indeed aligning LLMs to specialize in this specific genre of humor may not be found funny by many other populations in the world. However, as every comedian delivers jokes tailored to their audiences, we would argue aligning LLMs to humor of the New Yorker crowd is a valid task. As a future work and outside of the scope of this paper, many other genres of humor are yet to be studied for different demographics and cultures.

I am still slightly concerned about your definition of "funniness" as a population level variable (from this response):

So I would like to see a careful discussion of that somewhere in the paper - especially the motivations and limitations for this operationalisation approach to humour and funniness. I don't see it in the revised introduction PDF but trust that the authors will build this nuance in a camera-ready version.

For example, I'd like to know: is there any psychological or sociological basis for this population-level approach to defining "funniness"? 

I also think its critical to ask: what are some intended and unintended consequences of training a model with RLHF or direct alignment algorithm approaches to be "funnier" based on a "mean" or "generic" human? It seems like it might flatten or homogenise humour. You could look to some references outside of classic computer science literature, on how algorithmic presentation of culture (art, humour, music etc) affects population tastes.

Thank you for providing insightful feedback and supporting our work. We would like to address your concerns below.

Regards to your concerns about the data ownership. A subset of authors on this paper have run the crowdsourcing aspect of the New Yorker Caption Contest for the last nine years and collected the data directly, making a portion of it available at (https://nextml.github.io/caption-contest-data/). Past papers (eg. Hessel et al.) used the data at this link - in particular, Hessel et al. did not own/release the dataset, instead they employed it. To make this data more available to the community, provide context on it, and employ best practices, we have uploaded a copy to Hugging Face as described in Appendix A, and released this benchmark paper. We remark that our relationship with the New Yorker has ended, so this dataset will not be growing any further. 

**Introduction Revision**

While the introduction was actually written by an author, we agree with the reviewer that it sounds more like a funding proposal than a paper introduction. We have therefore toned down the introduction and added some of the details. Our introduction revision is attached as a pdf. 


**Subjectivity vs Objectivity**

Thank you for pointing out this confusion. In essence, subjectivity is on an individual level – the decision of whether a caption is funny varies from person to person. On the other hand, we objectively define funniness on the population level – more people find caption A funny than caption B. We can think of this as a binary random variable (e.g. whether or not an individual thinks a caption is funny), and "funniness" is simply the population mean of this random variable. Thus, though humor is subjective at a personal level, we can quantify it at a population level. In particular, we can ask how well LLM's can predict funny captions that would be enjoyed by the population on average. We can also ask how the population itself, or a human expert would do at this task. We will clarify this in the paper. 

Regarding L274 and Table 4. The standard error across six workers was 7.28%. This supports our main point that humans (expert and workers) prefer human generated captions to Claude generated captions. 


**Addressing "Definitional Clarity and Method Details"**

Thank you for the questions. We answer some of them here and address the rest in the revised introduction attached as the pdf for this rebuttal. We also would like to point the reviewer to the supplementary pdf material on OpenReview, as it contains the appendices and much of the information the reviewer is asking for.

1. What are we aligning to? As discussed above, we are aligning LLMs to generate and evaluate captions that are deemed funny collectively by the New Yorker readers. We have also modified the intro to incorporate this.

2. What is humor? We define a caption as funnier if the New Yorker readers found it funnier on average.

3. As mentioned, we have modified our intro.
4. We have clarified what a contest is in the revised intro.
5. L182, we used a group of human raters. L230, yes these are using 5-shot in context learning prompts. 
6. L140, prompt used is in Appendix B.3
5. Which task has been studied widely? Humor prediction, especially pairwise comparisons.
6. How do LLMs generate captions without images? As we mentioned on Line 142-145, we provide a description of the cartoon along with other detailed information in text.



**Other Examples...: Group Comparisons**

While group comparisons are not a novel technique in statistics and psychology, applying them to LLMs for this humor evaluation task is new. Previous conclusions drawn by Hessel et al. [19] is LLMs can only judge humor with less than 70% accuracy. The group comparison technique, when novelly applied to this task, can improve the accuracy to almost 80%, making the evaluation by LLMs much more reliable and feasible.

**Missing Documentation**

We refer the reviewer to the supplementary material pdf on OpenReview for Appendix A. Specifically for dataset documentation, the reviewer can find the dataset card (as a recommended documentation template in the call for datasets and benchmarks) at https://huggingface.co/datasets/yguooo/newyorker_caption_ranking. We were prohibited by law to track the New Yorker readers’ demographic information, so it is difficult to provide a concrete answer there. There is also no explicit instruction given to the New Yorker readers. They were only presented with three buttons as shown in Figure 2. For the human study for pairwise comparisons, we have included their instructions in Appendix C.

**Relation to Prior Work**

1. Hessel et al focused on tasks that highlight aspects of understanding, for example having an LLM explain why a joke is funny. We instead focus on generating captions and creating a benchmark for this task. We can't comment on the importance of understanding humor for generating humor (though agree that it is quite interesting). 
2. We meant that their effectiveness has not been well studied for creative tasks. We will clarify.
3. Thank you.
4. We added all large scale datasets with human ratings at the time the paper was written.
5. We will add an additional section reviewing some recent works at the intersection of Humour and LLMs in the appendix.

Thank you for providing insightful feedback and supporting our work. We would like to address your concerns below.

**Fairness Concerns: LLM with description vs VLM with cartoon images**

Information-wise, an image contains richer information than the description and entities–the information given to the pure LLM–as the latter can be deduced from images. Therefore, we would argue that the MLLMs in our experiments receive more information than the LLMs. Furthermore, both the LLM and MLLM are prompted with identical prompts, and no explicit chain-of-thought reasoning is performed. The difference in performance between an LLM and MLLM in our experiments is then due to the ability of each to evaluate and generate humor based on the given information, which is precisely what our experiments hope to measure. While the comparison between the LLM and MLLM does indeed introduce a different axis of variability than our other experiments, we believe this is an interesting axis to investigate, and believe our experiments to be fair.

Nonetheless, to better isolate the effects of vision, we have run the following additional experiments:

> a) GPT4-Turbo as evaluator given GPT4o descriptions (as reported in Table 2). This has an accuracy of 67%.

> b) GPT4-Turbo-vision as evaluator given both cartoon and GPT4o descriptions. This has an accuracy of 60.5%.

> c)GPT4-Turbo-vision as evaluator given both a blank image and GPT4o descriptions. This has an accuracy of 61.5%.

In particular, in (b) and (c) we give an MLLM the same text information as the pure LLM models, and find that it still performs worse. This suggests that the performance loss when using an MLLM is not due just to the type of information the MLLM is given (e.g. image vs text), but is due to other properties of MLLMs. We believe this motivates additional research in better integrating multimodal capabilities into large models. Given the discrepancy we observe on humor generation between text + vision vs vision-only models, we hope that our humor benchmark will provide a useful test case for measuring progress on this task.


**Evaluation Limitations: Reliability of Evaluation**

We respectfully disagree with the assertion that current models are inadequate for humor evaluation. Our group comparison technique achieves 80% accuracy within a reasonable budget, significantly outperforming individual human workers (~60%). This demonstrates that our approach is effective for evaluating funny captions.

It's crucial to distinguish between humor understanding (evaluation) and humor generation. While state-of-the-art models may underperform humans in generating humor, with our group comparison method, current LLMs do significantly outperform humans in judging. As evidenced by other tangential research literature such as [1], [2], and [3], LLMs are relatively better at judging than generation.

On the other hand, while expert evaluators achieve higher accuracy, this approach is neither scalable nor feasible as a practical benchmark. Our method strikes a balance between accuracy and practicality. As outlined in our future work section, we are developing gamified platforms to engage a broader user base in rating captions, which will further enhance our evaluation techniques. However, it's important to emphasize that our current group comparison method already provides a reliable and adequate assessment of humor evaluation tasks.


[1] Li, X., Zhang, T., Dubois, Y., Taori, R., Gulrajani, I., Guestrin, C., ... & Hashimoto, T. B. (2023). Alpacaeval: An automatic evaluator of instruction-following models.

[2] Zhong, V., Misra, D., Yuan, X., & Côté, M. A. (2024). Policy improvement using language feedback models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2402.07876.

[3] Saunders, W., Yeh, C., Wu, J., Bills, S., Ouyang, L., Ward, J., & Leike, J. (2022). Self-critiquing models for assisting human evaluators. arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.05802.

Thank you for providing insightful feedback and supporting our work. We would like to address your concerns below.

**Qualitative Insights**

Thank you for the great suggestion. We would like to include the following qualitative analysis about the caption generation in the final version of our paper.

We observe three types of common failure cases of LLMs in humor generation. We use the same cartoon as in Figure 2 for demonstration.

- *Missing visual details resulting in LLMs generating out-of-context captions.*
As an example, for the cartoon in Figure 2, GPT4o-vision generated “So the alien abduction statistics were right. Malls are the prime hunting grounds!”. This caption does not match the cartoon though, since the aliens look missing and worried. Their bodies look skinny and weak. In other words, they don’t seem to be here to hunt humans.

- *Many generated captions are forms of word/phrase modification and creation.* An example of this caption is “Do they have a Black Hole Friday sale?” from GPT4o-vision. Another example from Claude 3 opus is “I don't see 'Invasion Supplies' listed anywhere...” Both of these captions are inventing new words and phrases to make the caption funny. While these can be somewhat funny, they are usually not rated highly by the new yorker audiences.

- *Winning captions tend to appeal to readers with multiple interpretations through different lenses. LLMs currently lack the ability to produce such captions.* The New Yorker’s editorial pick of the final caption was “Oh sure, now you look at a map.” While this caption makes fun of the aliens blaming each other, it also references the experience of a driver missing the direction but claiming they knew the way. On the contrary, GPT4o-vision generated the caption “We travel light-years, and we still need directions!”, which despite making fun of the characters in the cartoon with the same concept, lacks the relatability from an additional perspective.

Overall, we think the GPT4 models are capable of generating humorous content. However, to rank among the top requires much deeper understanding of cultural references and more steps of reasoning before arriving at a high quality caption. We will include this discussion and include more examples for other cartoons in the final version of our paper.


**More investigation on VLMs vs LLMs**

We agree with the reviewer that the discrepancy between VLMs and LLMs is an interesting take-away from our results. To further investigate how VLMs behave when given both images and descriptions, we compared the following three methods on pairwise rankings:

> a) GPT4-Turbo as an evaluator given GPT4o descriptions (as reported in Table 2). This has an accuracy of 67%.

> b) GPT4-Turbo-vision as an evaluator given both cartoon and GPT4o descriptions. This has an accuracy of 60.5%.

> c) GPT4-Turbo-vision as an evaluator given both a blank image and GPT4o descriptions. This has an accuracy of 61.5%.

In particular, for (b) and (c), we are running the exact same model, the only difference is that one has access to the cartoon + text description, while the other has access only to the text description, thus isolating the effect of the image on the generation quality. We find that the visual element integration into the LLMs is negatively biasing the model’s accuracy. This observation is also consistent for overall and best pick group comparisons. Since giving a blank image also hurts performance compared to (a), GPT4 without vision, it is unlikely that the performance of the vision model is dragged down by the visual understanding capabilities. This suggests there is still much research to be done in better integrating multimodal capabilities into large models. Given the discrepancy we observe on humor generation between text + vision vs vision-only models, we hope that our humor benchmark will provide a useful test case for measuring progress on this task.

**Clarification on number of contests**

We experimented on 358 contests as those were the only ones available at the time we started our experiments. In total there are 365 contests released, which also include the contest that was hosted during the week of submission deadline.


**Summary Statistics and High-Level Details**

Thank you for this suggestion. We will use our additional content page in the camera ready version to add these details.

summary_and_contributions.value:
- The paper presents a novel dataset that indicates human preferences regarding cartoon captions. The dataset could enable fine-tuning or aligning VLMs / LLMs to (1) generate humorous captions given an image, and (2) better estimate human preferences in humor-related tasks

- The large dataset contains 365 “The New Yorker” magazine’s cartoons, 2.2 million captions, and 250 million human ratings

- The paper also proposes a novel ranking evaluation that combines human judgements (typically used) with LLM results. While absolute scores for data samples are easier to obtain, ranking is a more natural task (and metric) for ambiguous, subjective tasks 

- The paper confirms that state-of-the-art LLMs / VLMs (GPT4, Claude) underperform human contestants in generating humorous captions, highlighting a clear avenue for improvement in these models. They also experiment with, and establish that a few current fine-tuning methods don’t directly solve the problem of generating humorous captions.

review.value:
The paper’s main contribution is a larger-scale dataset compared to the existing New Yorker cartoons and captions. 

The paper also presents interesting evaluations of LLMs and VLMs, in addition to results from fine-tuning / alignment experiments with RLHF and DPO. The overall findings indicate that models are often better than lay persons at understanding humor, but fall short of experts by a significant level. 

Please see the other sections for pros / cons and questions.

strengths.value:
- The scale of the dataset is orders of magnitudes larger than existing datasets on human preference ratings, and multi-modal humor (captions). This is an important contribution in the line of computational humor works

- Unlike typical academic datasets, the data presented here was voluntarily generated – during a cartoon caption over a period of 8 years. The quality of such a dataset will likely surpass other academic works where laypersons (e.g., on Amazon Mechanical Turk) are forced to generate humorous content, and provide their humor judgements

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
Experiments on VLMs -- the most surprising take-away from the paper is that the VLMs are outperformed by LLMs. This is a topic that would be really interesting to study in more depth. In what specific cases do the LLMs outperform VLMs? Is this due to the low or high visual complexity of the image? Are there elements / characteristics of the captions themselves that contribute to being a funny caption? 

Quantitative results are obviously critical to evaluating the performance of different models and acquiring a summary-statistic regarding the entire dataset. However, it would be really interesting to have a more detailed analysis of the specific modes of success and failure of the different approaches. 

What new insights can we gain from the experiments in this paper, specifically regarding linguistic and visual understanding of humorous images?

limitations.value:
- Despite the large number of captions and ratings, the dataset seems to contain only 365 unique images. This limits the diversity in terms of topics, style of humor, etc. However, this limitation is completely understandable -- it is extremely challenging to acquire high quality humorous data in large volume

- Limited novelty in the dataset. The main contribution of the paper is the dataset. However the specific format of the cartoons, captions, and human ratings aren't new to the community. Despite this, the scale of the dataset is much larger, and the updated analysis on the latest LLMs are of interest

correctness.value:
The paper performs interesting experiments and analyses. In addition, it also clearly identifies specific points that would be good to explore in the future. These are explicitly marked as "Proposed Research Question", which serves as food for thought for the reader. 

A question that came up from early on while reading the draft: How many images exactly are part of the dataset? One image per contest? So, 365 overall? It might be nice to explicitly mention this early on in the paper.

clarity.value:
The paper is well-written and the dataset description is clear

Minor point: L146 mentions 358 contests -- can the authors please clarify the exact number of contests in the dataset -- 365 vs. 358?

relation_to_prior_work.value:
The dataset (images, captions, ratings) itself is not really novel to the community. Prior works have released parts of the same dataset, albeit in smaller scales (less than 50 images). The paper briefly discusses prior work that presents a similar dataset, and tasks. The key features that distinguishes the current submission are: 

(1) Scale of dataset (about an order of magnitude larger in terms of number of contests) 

(2) Fine-tuning experiments (e.g., attempting to align LLMs with RLHF leveraging the human preference ratings in the dataset)

documentation.value:

It would nevertheless be useful to have some summary statistics and high-level details in the paper itself.

title.value: A novel multimodal preference dataset for humor alignment of LLMs and MLLMs

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces a dataset and benchmark for evaluating the humor generation capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). The dataset consists of over 250 million human ratings on more than 2.2 million captions collected from The New Yorker's weekly cartoon caption contest. The benchmark utilizes GPT-4 and human judgments to evaluate model-generated captions and explores various alignment strategies, including RLHF and DPO. The study reveals limitations of current fine-tuning methods in creative tasks and demonstrates that even state-of-the-art models like GPT-4 and Claude currently underperform top human contestants in generating humorous captions.

review.value:
Pros:
1. The massive-scale, crowd-sourced dataset with human judgments is a unique resource for studying humor generation in LLMs. The benchmark provides a standardized framework for evaluating humor in AI-generated content, addressing the limitations of subjective evaluation methods.

2. The study reveals valuable insights into the current capabilities and limitations of LLMs in humor generation, guiding future research and development. The analysis of different alignment strategies provides valuable insights into their effectiveness for humor generation, informing the development of more effective approaches.

3. The paper is well-written and presents a clear and thorough analysis of the humor generation capabilities of LLMs. The figures and tables are informative and clearly illustrate the key findings. The appendices provide additional details and clarify the experimental setup.

Cons:
1.  The study primarily focuses on humor generation in the context of cartoon captions. It would be interesting to explore the generalizability of the findings to other creative tasks.

strengths.value:
1. The study addresses the critical gap in understanding and evaluating the humor generation capabilities of LLMs, which is essential for developing AI systems that can effectively engage with human values and preferences.

2. The study is relevant to a broad range of research communities, including natural language processing, machine learning, AI alignment, and creativity research. The findings have practical implications for developers and designers of AI systems, guiding the creation of more engaging and entertaining AI-generated content.


3. The paper employs a sound methodology, utilizing a large-scale dataset, novel evaluation metrics, and a systematic comparison of alignment strategies. The results are well-explained and supported by evidence, providing a comprehensive understanding of the current state of humor generation in LLMs.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: The study primarily focuses on humor generation for cartoon captions, which may not be fully representative of humor generation in other domains. Expanding the evaluation or discussions to other creative tasks and humor genres would provide a more comprehensive understanding of LLM capabilities and offer additional insights for readers.

limitations.value: The authors have discussed the limitations in the paper.

correctness.value: The dataset is constructed through a sound process of collecting human ratings on cartoon captions from The New Yorker’s caption contest. The use of a multi-armed bandit algorithm for presenting captions to raters ensures efficient identification of the best captions. The paper introduces novel evaluation methods, including group comparison techniques utilizing GPT-4 and human judgments. These methods address the subjectivity of humor and provide a more reliable and objective framework for evaluating humor generation.

clarity.value: The paper is well-written, providing a comprehensive analysis of the humor generation capabilities of LLMs. The figures and tables effectively convey the key findings, and the appendices offer supplementary details.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The paper has discussed its relation to prior work in several sections, highlighting the differences and contributions of the current study, including New Yorker caption contest, alignment of LLMs, and RLHF datasets.

documentation.value: The paper mentions the use of a multi-armed bandit algorithm for collecting human ratings and describes the process of filtering captions by the New Yorker’s editorial staff. In addition, the paper provides a URL for accessing the dataset on Hugging Face. However, it would be helpful to provide more details about the specific criteria used for filtering. In addition, it would be beneficial to include information about the intended uses of the dataset and any restrictions on its use (currently are empty in https://huggingface.co/datasets/yguooo/newyorker_caption_ranking). Additionally, it would be helpful to know if there are plans for maintaining and updating the dataset in the future.

title.value: Review for Humor in AI: Massive Scale Crowd-Sourced Preferences and Benchmarks for Cartoon Captioning

summary_and_contributions.value:
This paper presents a large-scale dataset and new benchmarks to improve AI's ability to generate humorous captions. Based on this preference data, the paper analyzes state-of-the-art models (e.g., GPT-4, Claude), showing they still underperform compared to human humor generation, and examines methods like RLHF and DPO for better aligning AI outputs with human preferences.

The contributions of the paper are:

1. Large-Scale Dataset Creation: Introduced a novel multimodal preference dataset with over 250 million human ratings on 2.2 million captions from The New Yorker’s cartoon caption contest.

2. Benchmark Development: Established new benchmarks for evaluating the quality of AI-generated humorous captions using advanced models like GPT-4.

3. Performance Evaluation of Models: Analyzed the performance of state-of-the-art models (e.g., GPT-4, Claude) in generating humorous content, demonstrating their limitations compared to human contestants.

4. Examination of Alignment Strategies: Assessed various alignment strategies, including Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Best-of-N sampling (BoN), for improving humor generation in LLMs.

5. Open-Source Contribution: Made the dataset and code publicly available to support further research in AI humor generation and evaluation.

review.value:
- **Originality**: The paper introduces a novel large-scale dataset focused on humor generation, which is a valuable resource for the research community. This dataset is unique in its scale and focus on creative AI tasks, offering new opportunities for research and development in the field of AI humor.

- **Quality**: The paper is well-written and provides a comprehensive analysis of the performance of state-of-the-art models and alignment methods in humor generation. The analysis is supported by empirical results and reveals the limitations of current approaches, providing a detailed examination of the strengths and weaknesses of models like GPT-4 and Claude.

- **Clarity**: The paper is well-structured and clearly presents datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation results. The writing is easy to follow, and the figures and tables are well-organized, enhancing the readability and understanding of the complex information provided.

- **Significance**: The paper provides a novel tasks to evaluate AI-generated humor, which is unexplored in the field of LLM and alignment. The introduction of new benchmarks and alignment strategies offers valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities for improving AI humor generation, contributing to the advancement of creative AI research.

### Evaluation:

#### Pros:
1. **Unique Dataset:** Introduction of an extensive dataset with over 250 million human ratings on cartoon captions, providing a rich resource for studying humor in AI.
2. **Novel Benchmarks:** Development of new evaluation metrics for AI-generated humor, offering a standardized framework for future research.
3. **Comprehensive Analysis:** Detailed performance evaluation of state-of-the-art models and alignment methods, backed by empirical results.
4. **Alignment Strategies:** Exploration of methods like RLHF and DPO for better aligning AI outputs with human preferences, offering insights into potential improvements.
5. **Open-Source Contribution:** Public availability of the dataset and code encourages further research and collaboration in the field.

#### Cons:
1. **Fairness Concerns:** Language-only models are provided with descriptions and object entities of cartoons, potentially biasing the comparison with multimodal models. The comparison of language-only models with multimodal models may not be entirely fair, as the former may benefit from additional information like chain of thought prompt.
2. **Evaluation Limitations:** The paper highlights the underperformance of state-of-the-art models compared to human humor generation, raising questions about the adequacy of current models for humor evaluation.

strengths.value:
This paper is well-written and provides an important contribution to the field of AI humor generation. It reveals the substantial gap between AI-generated humor and human-created humor. The introduction of a large-scale dataset with over 250 million human ratings on cartoon captions offers a valuable resource for the research community. Additionally, the paper also compares the performance of state-of-the-art models and alignment strategies, providing insights into the current challenges and potential improvements in AI humor generation.
development of new benchmarks for evaluating AI-generated humor establishes a standardized framework for future studies. Furthermore, the open-source availability of the dataset and code encourages collaboration and further innovation in AI humor generation.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. This paper mentioned that the state-of-the-art models still underperform compared to human humor generation. Therefore, it is doubtful whether the GPT-4 are sufficient to evaluate the humor generation capability of AI.
2. As mentioned in the paper, the language-only models are provided the descriptions and object entities of the cartoons. Thus, it is not fair to compare the performance of language-only models with multimodal models.

summary_and_contributions.value:
* Release large dataset to the community (2.2 million captions, 250 million human ratings) for future research. Code and data is said to be available.
* Demonstrate methodological weaknesses in existing approaches, like DPO and RLHF, but applied to a slightly new setting (humour) where the human preference rules may differ from helpfulness, honesty or harmlessness (or other commonly targeted attributes)
* I am slightly uncertain how the contributions of this paper interacts with the hosters of the New York Caption Contest. Are they the owners or curators of the original data or rely on that existing data? How did Hessel et al., use the data before? Was it open-source, and did they also release a dataset? review.value:
**Pros**
* I summarise this in the “Strengths” section of the review.

**Cons are listed thematically**

**LLM-style writing and over-claims or vagueness in language**
* This paper does read as fairly LLM-heavy in writing - e.g., “delve”, “foster an understanding”, “sheds light on” etc. I would encourage the authors to simplify their writing slightly for cleaner, more technical language.
* “_The dataset has already catalyzed groundbreaking research_” - While one follow-up paper may have impressively won an ACL award, sentences like this are unnecessarily overclaimed and weaken the appeal of the paper.
* L30-L39 - feels particularly “LLM” style of writing. Given this section “Dataset” is meant to be summarising your core contribution, it would benefit from less general abstract sentences and more clear details.
* L41 - introduces novel techniques… “_leveraging cutting-edge techniques such_ as GPT”. Again, I’m not sure leveraging GPT is a cutting-edge technique in today’s research landscape. These words and space could be used to describe how you use GPT. 
* Similarly, In L40, you introduce the Benchmark but without many clear technical or data details, the space or word count is instead used for sentences like “By establishing this benchmark, the paper not only enhances our understanding of humor in AI systems but also paves the way for more rigorous and systematic evaluations in the future.”
* Same applies to the other paragraphs in intro - Generative Capabilities of SOTA models (L46) and Alignment Strategy Evaluation (L53).
* I would advise a heavy rewrite of the introduction is required for this paper to be of sufficient standard for this track. At current, there is lacking precision in the communication.

**Other examples of over-claiming language**
* I would avoid comments like “we introduce the novel group comparison technique”. How is it novel to ask annotators to go from pairwise to group comparisons? That is a methodological design decision but not a “novel” contribution (in my understanding). If it is truly novel, then explain why.

**Definitional Clarity and Method Details**
* “to investigate alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs)” - opening line of intro. Can you include a definition of alignment as you mean it here? What are you investigating as it relates to alignment?
* Similarly can you provide a clear definition of what is “humour” (as you operationalise it)
* Sentences like this “This research aims to foster the development of more reliable, capable, and aligned AI systems, ultimately advancing the field of AI alignment and its practical applications” (L28) are unhelpful and too general. How does your research make LLMs more reliable? How does it make them more capable? You have a good setting but the introduction is weakened by too general and abstract phrases like this. 
* What is a “contest”? (Figure 1 caption)
* L182 - in evals, you provide the query to “_an LLM/human rater_” - Is it a single human-rater? Or a group of human raters?
* L230 - “_We also evaluate state-of-the-art close-sourced models including GPT4o and Claude 3 Opus._” - I assume this is just prompting given these models can’t be fine-tuned.
* In L140, When you say the model was “_asked to generate funny captions about it._” - what prompt was used?
* In L172, you say “_This task has been studied widely_”. What “task” are you refering to? Humour prediction?
* L238 - I am confused about a method detail in L238 - “Surprisingly, language-only models such as the pretrained Mistral model outperform the multimodal LLaVa model that has access to the entire cartoon images”.  I maybe missed a method detail but how would an LLM give a caption without seeing the image? This feels like a critical weakness of the setup if the LLM does not have a representation of the image it is captioning.

**Conceptual clarity on the objectivity vs subjectivity of humour (and small sample sizes)**
* In L43 you say “standardized framework for assessing humor in AI-generated content, enabling precise and objective evaluations compared to traditional subjective methods”. In L16 (only a few paragraphs earlier), you motivate your setting by saying “The task of writing funny captions comes with significant challenges due to subjectivity and variability in human judgments.” Which is true? How is it possible to have precise and objective evaluations in an area which you say is fundamentally subjective? This is a big weakness of the framing of the paper.
* You start section 4.2 which a quote about how subjective humour is. But later you make statements like “models outperform average humans (crowd workers) in judging the funniness across all three _comparison settings_” (L189). If humour is so subjective, is the concept of a mean human rater meaningful? How can you “outperform” human raters if humour ratings are subjective? Similarly, how does the concept of a “human expert” content with humour subjectivity? At the moment, the paper’s framing sits between arguing humour is very subjective but then applying objective lens and metrics. A clearer positioning is needed.
* Furthermore, you only use 6 human workers for the eval in 274. I’m glad you do include a custom human eval but this is a small sample size for judging a very subjective task. What was the variance or noise among workers? Can you give an estimate of subjective disagreement? 

**Missing Documentation**
* Unless the authors have not attached the dataset documentation to the main paper (as I think the instructions advised), I do not see any documentation of the dataset. They mention an Appendix A but it is not in the PDF. This could be an error. However, at current it is a big issue because the paper itself does not contain sufficient detail e.g., on annotator demographics, or annotation instructions, nor is there any formal documentation e.g., data statement (Bender et al.,) or datasheet (Gebru et al.,).

strengths.value:
* Relatively well-written (especially after the Intro)
* Releases a large and interesting dataset, which I can see being of interest to future researchers.
* Paints a comprehensive “lifecycle” of the issue at hand - e..g,  covers all elements of the cycle from data, to training, to human/LLM-as-a-judge eval.
* Table 3 demonstrates the strengths of this paper - carefully designed comparisons across multiple models.
* Section 4.3, Table 3 and Experiments (Section 5) are good.
* The section fine-tuning open source model has some valuable practical insights.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
These are summarised in my review.

Small grammar errors, sentence improvements or typos
* “Our exploration of alignment in LLMs through this dataset sheds light on fundamental questions regarding evaluation and alignment with human values and preferences” L19, could be improved.
* “updated a weekly basis for the last several years” - specify the years instead of “last several years” which is vague and hard for the reader to interpret if they read this paper e.g., in 2 years from now.
* L112 - “The contest began in 2005, and at the time this work was written, there have been roughly 900 contests.” - is contest plural or singular?

limitations.value: They have a very short discussion on limitations (probably because of space constraints). Same for negative societal impact-on offensiveness and toxicity. Generally I would like to see more of a discussion of the subjective-objective tensions mentioned in my review.

correctness.value: Yes, to my knowledge. It could be more clearly communicated in the introduction what the exact dataset and benchmark consist of, so future readers have a clear precise idea from the start.

clarity.value: Mixed - overall it is not hard to understand and there are very few typos or formatting errors. However, as per my review above, I think there is too much generic, vague and "LLM-sounding" language. I cannot say for sure an LLM was used to write large parts of the introduction, but it certainly feels that way as a reader because technical details are lost in place of very general statements.

relation_to_prior_work.value:
* Yes - they do discuss related work. I do have a question though. You suggest that a key different to prior work was their attempt to “understand” humour (L73). What does this mean? How was it operationalised? What does your work do instead? Is “understanding” humour critical for generating humour?
* “Despite extensive research into various fine-tuning methodologies, understanding their effectiveness remains nascent” - What is evidence for this claim? Without further caveating it is an overclaim. Perhaps there has been a lack of effectivness for creativity, but generally.
* Otherwise the “Alignment of LLMs” section is better. 
* “RLHF Datasets” - Somewhat ad-hoc what datasets were included here. How were they chosen? 
* I am missing a section of the related work on “Modelling Creativity in AI”, covering the body of work in the intersection of AI and humour.

title.value: Humor in AI: Massive Scale Crowd-Sourced Preferences and Benchmarks for Cartoon Captioning

abstract.value: We present a novel multimodal preference dataset for creative tasks, consisting of over 250 million human votes on more than 2.2 million captions, collected through crowdsourcing rating data for The New Yorker's weekly cartoon caption contest over the past eight years. This unique dataset supports the development and evaluation of multimodal large language models and preference-based fine-tuning algorithms for humorous caption generation. We propose novel benchmarks for judging the quality of model-generated captions, utilizing both GPT4 and human judgments to establish ranking-based evaluation strategies. Our experimental results highlight the limitations of current fine-tuning methods, such as RLHF and DPO, when applied to creative tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even state-of-the-art models like GPT4 and Claude currently underperform top human contestants in generating humorous captions. As we conclude this extensive data collection effort, we release the entire preference dataset to the research community, fostering further advancements in AI humor generation and evaluation.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
